title: Infra: GPU Fleet & Capacity — Cloud Accounts, Networking, IaC, CI/CD (Team Wiki)
author: Aisha Kapoor
body:
Summary

This team-wiki page consolidates the Infrastructure Engineering standards and runbooks for the GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC module design, and CI/CD pipelines used to build and ship infra changes. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners. Follow the operational runbooks for production actions; use the module patterns and CI/CD examples when authoring new IaC.

Sections
- Ownership and contacts
- Capacity targets and SLOs
- Cloud accounts & organizational structure
- Networking and VPC design standards

1) Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: infra-gpu-team (engineering)
- Pager & on-call: infra-oncall (see oncall rota in /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response)
- Primary contacts: Aisha Kapoor (infra lead), Gabriel Lee (capacity), Marta Rossi (networking)

2) Capacity targets and SLOs

Short intro: Our capacity planning balances steady-state reserved capacity (Dedicated) and burst on multi-tenant pools. Capacity decisions prioritize latency SLOs for hosted customers and cost efficiency for internal workloads.

SLOs and targets (examples):
- 99th percentile per-token latency for small requests (<=256 tokens): <= 120ms on dedicated pools
- Throughput target per GPU (A100/H100 equivalent): 60 concurrent small-chat streams
- Overprovisioning buffer: maintain 15% spare GPU slots per region during business hours
- Safety headroom for peak events: ability to add +25% capacity within 60 minutes using pre-allocated burst accounts

Capacity planning cadence:
1. Weekly capacity health check (metrics reviewed: utilization, queue length, tail latency, failed allocations)
2. Monthly forecast (based on bookings, usage trends, and upcoming customer rollouts)
3. Quarterly major procurement decisions (hardware refresh, reserved capacity contracts)

Required dashboards/metrics:
- GPU utilization by instance family and region
- Average/peak NVLink and PCIe bus utilization
- Queue length and batching efficiency
- Runtime OOM and model allocation failures

3) Cloud accounts & organizational structure

Principles:
- Use a multi-account design: org-root -> billing -> infra (shared services) -> prod -> staging -> dev -> customer-isolated accounts (for Private)
- Least-privilege IAM roles and cross-account roles for automation
- Centralized billing and tagging policies enforced by SCPs and Tag Policies

Required roles and policies (high level):
- infra-deploy-role@prod (full deploy permissions limited to IaC pipelines)
- infra-monitor-role (read-only monitoring + logs access)
- cross-account-operator (assume-role used by our CI/CD runner for customer onboarding)

Account setup checklist:
- Billing alarm configured and tested
- Centralized logging forwarder enabled (CloudWatch/Stackdriver -> central observability account)
- Config rules enabled (enforce encryption at rest, public S3 block, required tags)
- Network peering/Transit gateway set up for prod connectivity (see Networking section)

4) Networking and VPC design standards

Design principles:
- Each region has a transit VPC managed by infra-networking team; production clusters sit in prod VPCs peered via transit gateway
- Private subnets for GPU hosts with no internet-facing IPs; egress through NAT gateways or egress VPC endpoints if required
- Use security groups for host-level controls; NACLs for coarse subnet policies
- Use PrivateLink / VPC endpoints for datastore and observability integrations

Standard VPC layout (per region):
| Subnet Type | CIDR example | Purpose | Notes |
|-------------|--------------|---------|-------|
| mgmt-public | 10.10.0.0/24 | Bastion, admin access | Restricted via IP allowlists |
| prod-private-1 | 10.10.1.0/22 | GPU hosts AZ-a | No public IPs, NAT egress |
| prod-private-2 | 10.10.5.0/22 | GPU hosts AZ-b | As above |
| services | 10.10.9.0/24 | Metrics, logging endpoints | PrivateLink endpoints |

Networking requirements for GPU hosts:
- Support for SR-IOV or ENA tuned networking (depending on cloud)
- MTU >= 9000 where supported to reduce CPU overhead for large model transfers
- Dedicated ENIs per GPU host for data plane isolation (recommended)

Firewall and security groups example:
- sg-gpu-hosts: allow inbound from mgmt bastion (TCP 22), metrics collector (TCP 9090), orchestrator (TCP 8000), intra-cluster (custom high ports)
- sg-k8s-nodeport: restrict NodePort range to 30000-32767 and only allow from load balancer sg

5) Terraform / IaC modules & patterns

Module registry & naming conventions:
- Module names: rh-mod-<domain>-<purpose> (e.g., rh-mod-network-vpc, rh-mod-gpu-cluster, rh-mod-iam-roles)
- Versions: semantic (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and published to internal module registry (artifact repo)

Module patterns and best practices:
- Keep modules small and composable: separate vpc, subnets, route tables, security groups, and cluster as discrete modules
- Idempotency: modules must be safe to reapply and include meaningful lifecycle rules for ephemeral resources (avoid destroying unless explicitly requested)
- Input validation: provide input schema and limit ranges for CIDRs, instance types, and counts

Example modules table:
| Module | Purpose | Required inputs | Outputs |
|--------|---------|-----------------|---------|
| rh-mod-network-vpc | Create VPC, subnets, TGW attachments | region, cidr_block, azs | vpc_id, subnet_ids |
| rh-mod-gpu-cluster | Autoscaling group / k8s nodegroup for GPU hosts | vpc_id, subnet_ids, instance_type, desired_count | asg_id, nodegroup_name |
| rh-mod-iam-roles | Central IAM roles and policies | account_id, role_names | role_arns |

Example Terraform usage snippet:
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.2.0"
  required_providers {
    aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = ">= 4.0" }
  }
}

module "vpc" {
  source  = "internal/rh-mod-network-vpc/aws"
  version = "1.3.0"
  region  = var.region
  cidr_block = var.vpc_cidr
}

Module testing and validation:
- Unit tests: terraform validate + tflint + checkov in CI
- Integration test: spin up ephemeral account with the module and run smoke tests (create resources, verify outputs, destroy)

6) CI/CD and build pipelines for infra modules

Pipeline stages (recommended):
1. Pre-commit: fmt, lint, tflint, static checks
2. PR validation: terraform init & plan against a dry-run workspace; run unit tests and checkov
3. Integration test: For major modules, run ephemeral apply in a sandbox account (scheduled or PR-triggered for major changes)
4. Review and approval: required approvers for changes to prod-facing modules
5. Publish: publish module artifact to internal registry and bump module versions
6. Deploy: automated apply triggered by release pipeline to target accounts with controlled approvals

CI examples (GitHub Actions / GitLab):
- Use short-lived credentials (OIDC) and assume-role into target accounts for plan/apply
- Store state in central remote backend (S3/State Locking + DynamoDB) with strict encryption and ACLs

Pipeline security controls:
- Prevent direct pushes to main branch; require PR review and signed commits for module releases
- Approvals from infra owners for changes touching network, IAM, or production scaling logic

7) Runbooks (scaling, upgrades, incidents)

Runbook: Scale up GPU capacity (quick path)
1. Validate demand signal: review dashboard metrics (queue length, P99 latency, scheduling failures)
2. Check available burst accounts and quotas: verify cloud quota and pre-provisioned instance pool
3. Trigger autoscaling policy change: increase target ASG desired_count by X% (usually increments of 10-25%)
4. Monitor health: ensure new nodes register to k8s, run node-provisioning hooks, and pass healthchecks
5. Rebalance traffic: update routing policy in orchestrator to include new capacity
6. Post-incident: revert autoscaling change when stable and document timeline in incident tracker

Runbook: Drain and replace GPU host during kernel/driver upgrade
1. Mark node as unschedulable: kubectl cordon <node>
2. Evict pods gracefully: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120
3. Verify pods rescheduled and healthchecks passing
4. Perform host maintenance (apt/yum update, driver install, reboot)
5. Run post-maint checks: dmesg, nvidia-smi, container runtime health
6. Uncordon node: kubectl uncordon <node>

Runbook: OOM / model allocation failure triage
1. Identify failing pods/nodes via logs and metrics (OOMKilled, allocation errors)
2. Check model size and quantization profile requested; fallback to smaller quantized variant if available
3. If due to noisy neighbor, throttle offending tenant or move to isolated pool
4. If systemic, scale up capacity temporarily and open incident with infra-sre

8) Onboarding checklist for new GPU hardware or region

Pre-procurement:
- Capacity forecast and cost approval
- Validate vendor compatibility (NVLINK, interconnects) and cloud region availability

Pre-deployment:
- Create region account and required IAM roles
- Create VPC and transit gateway attachments
- Publish IaC modules for the new instance types (machine image + kernel config)
- Add to monitoring dashboards and set alert thresholds

Deployment validation:
- Run perf benchmark suite (latency/throughput) using internal benchmarking harness
- Verify batching and KV cache behavior against typical workloads
- Conduct a canary run with limited traffic for 24-72 hours

Appendix: Quick commands and snippets

Assume deploy role (example - AWS OIDC):
aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/infra-deploy-role --role-session-name ci-pipeline-session

Terraform plan (CI step):
terraform init -backend-config="bucket=my-terraform-state" -backend-config="dynamodb_table=terraform-locks"
terraform plan -var-file=ci.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan

K8s drain node example:
kubectl cordon gpu-node-01
kubectl drain gpu-node-01 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120

Notes and governance
- Major changes to network topology, IAM roles, or scaling logic require ADR and review by infra-architecture and security teams
- Keep runbooks up to date after each incident and annotate the runbook with a postmortem link
